approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, the Douglas Creek alder, then the west-side gully to the polished slabs
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Easy Pass trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 151, about 3,700 ft. Hike 3.5 miles and 2,800 ft to Easy Pass at 6,500 ft, then descend 1.5 miles through alpine meadows and forest into Fisher Basin and down to the Fisher Creek valley floor and the established campsites.

Cross Fisher Creek on a large fallen log and travel the east side of the Douglas Creek valley on a faint climbers' path. This is where the route is actually decided. The transition from forest to open terrain runs into a vast field of slide alder and brush over ten feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, cut by small rocky stream channels — progress measured in inches per minute. One 2022 party was turned back at 4,200 ft by this alone, having covered half a mile an hour for seven hours. The glacier travel is superb and the bushwhack miserable.

Above the brush, the way onto the glacier is a gully on the west side of the basin. Then it is glacier travel to the col and a short summit block.
approach_variants.season: June and July for the best glacier conditions
hazards: A slide-alder thicket over ten feet high that has defeated at least one party outright, with heavy mosquito and black-fly pressure
Cliff bands ringing the Fisher Basin cirque
Crevasses and glide cracks reported over 20 ft deep on the Douglas Glacier
A steep, exposed rock ramp of roughly 300 ft above camp that is hard to protect
Steep icy summit snow needing solid crampon and axe technique
Steep loose-rock switchbacks on the Easy Pass trail itself above mile 2.5
approach_variants.baseFinding: The gully is on the west side of the basin and it is identified by what it delivers you onto, not by its entrance. It starts class 3, steepens quickly to class 4 or low fifth for a short section that is hard to protect, and tops out on glacier-polished slabs. Polished slabs above a short steep step is the confirmation. From there it is about 1,500 vertical ft of scrambling on those slabs to the toe of the Douglas Glacier. So the order is: brush, gully, polished slabs, glacier. If you are on slabs without having climbed a short hard step, you have not been through the gully. The route joins its neighbour near the top and that is expected: ascend the Douglas Glacier — steep at its head — to the col, then traverse to meet the Banded Glacier and finish up the same class 3-4 summit block, about 300 vertical ft. A summit block reached without crossing to a second glacier means you are still on the Douglas side of the col. The approach is the strongest discriminator on this mountain, because all three routes end at the same summit but none of them share a valley. This route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek drainage on the west. The Banded Glacier comes from Fisher Creek to a lake camp at 5,160 ft and crosses a col onto the Banded. The Fremont Glacier comes from Thunder Creek and Park Creek Pass on the southeast. If you passed Park Creek Pass this morning, you are not on the Douglas. And the honest gap: no source publishes a countable marker for the gully entrance itself — it is described only as being on the west side of the basin. The polished slabs above it are the reliable confirmation, which means you find out you were right after the hard part.
